question: Why is OpenAI Whisper generally a poor choice for real-time voice AI despite its excellent accuracy?
options: Because it does not support any languages besides English
Because it cannot process audio longer than 30 seconds
Because it is more expensive than other providers
Because it was designed for batch transcription, resulting in 500-1000ms latency that is far too high for conversational voice AI
explanation: Whisper was designed for batch processing. Its 500-1000ms latency for first results is far too high for real-time voice AI where sub-second end-to-end response times are required. Streaming-first providers like Deepgram deliver partial results in ~100ms.

question: Why is function calling reliability considered the most critical LLM capability for agentic voice AI?
options: Because function calling determines the LLM's response quality
Because all voice AI agents require at least ten function tools
Because a failed function call leaves the user in awkward silence with no easy recovery, unlike text chatbots where users can retry
Because function calling is the most expensive LLM feature
explanation: In text chatbots, a function calling failure is recoverable — the user can retry or rephrase. In voice AI, a failure results in awkward silence or incorrect behavior with no easy way to recover. This makes reliable function calling essential for production voice agents.

question: Why is time-to-first-byte (TTFB) more important than peak voice quality (MOS score) when choosing a TTS provider for voice AI?
options: Because higher MOS scores always indicate slower processing
Because TTFB directly impacts total latency — every millisecond of TTS delay adds to the time before the user hears a response
Because users cannot perceive voice quality differences
Because TTFB determines TTS processing cost
explanation: In a streaming pipeline, TTS latency directly adds to end-to-end response time. A 100-200ms TTFB difference is perceptible and significant. While voice quality differences between top providers are subtle (4.0-4.4 MOS), latency differences directly impact whether the conversation feels natural.

question: What is the 'swap test' pattern and why does LiveKit's architecture make it particularly easy?
options: It swaps between pipeline mode and realtime mode during a conversation
It tests multiple models simultaneously and merges their outputs
It keeps two pipeline components fixed and swaps the third to isolate the impact of each provider — with LiveKit Inference, swapping means changing one model string
It automatically selects the fastest provider at runtime
explanation: The swap test keeps two components fixed (e.g., STT and LLM) and changes only the third (e.g., TTS). With LiveKit Inference, swapping means changing one model string. With plugins, it means changing one import and one line. This isolates the impact of each provider for clean comparison.
